title: Cartan subgroups generate a connected affine algebraic group
statement: Let $k$ be an infinite field [def-weil-field], and let $G$ be a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], geometrically connected [def-weil-connected-scheme], affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Closed subgroup schemes mean [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], tori mean [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type], and maximal tori mean [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. Write $C_G(T)$ for the closed subgroup representing the centralizer functor of [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected]. The collection of maximal $k$-tori of $G$ is nonempty. For every closed $k$-subgroup scheme $H\subseteq G$, if $C_G(T)\subseteq H$ for every maximal $k$-torus $T\subseteq G$, then $H=G$ as closed subgroup schemes. No smoothness or connectedness assumption is imposed on $H$, and no reductivity or perfectness assumption is imposed on $G$ or $k$.

source.place: Theorem 17.91, printed p.381 (generation); Corollary 17.83 and its proof, printed p.379 (existence of a maximal torus). Generation is the smallest-closed-subgroup notion introduced in section 2h, printed pp.53-56.

proof.text: We first record the dimension test used below. If $J\subseteq V$ is a closed subgroup of a smooth geometrically connected affine finite-type group and $\dim J=\dim V$, then $J=V$, even if $J$ is not smooth. Extend to $\bar k$. The identity-local-dimension and rational-point base-change statements identify both group dimensions with those before extension. Smoothness is preserved and $V_{\bar k}$ is reduced. The identity-component theorem makes the connected $V_{\bar k}$ irreducible. The affine dimension-drop theorem therefore forces the closed subset $|J_{\bar k}|$ to equal $|V_{\bar k}|$. If $I$ is its defining ideal in the reduced coordinate algebra, then every element of $I$ belongs to every prime, hence is zero. Thus $I=0$. Finally a $k$-vector space maps injectively to its tensor product with $\bar k$ (extend a basis), so the original defining ideal is zero too.

source.place: Sections 1.34–1.37, pp.16–18; 10.15, pp.190–191; dimension argument underlying 17.77 and 17.91. Expanded scheme-theoretic dimension test.

proof.text: There is at least the trivial torus in $G$. Dimensions of torus subgroups are integers between $0$ and $\dim G$, since their underlying spaces are closed in $G$ and chains of irreducible closed subsets remain chains in $G$. Choose one of largest dimension. If it were strictly contained in another torus, the dimension test of step 1 applied with that torus as ambient group would rule out equal dimensions; hence the larger torus would have strictly larger dimension. This is impossible. This proves maximal-torus existence, also for every smooth connected group used below: such a group is geometrically connected because its identity is rational. A torus is geometrically reduced and geometrically connected: after any field extension, embed that field and a splitting field into an algebraically closed common overfield. Its coordinate algebra then becomes a Laurent polynomial ring, which is a domain. Injectivity of scalar extension forbids a nonzero nilpotent or a nontrivial idempotent before extension. The connectedness-idempotent criterion gives geometric connectedness, and the geometrically-reduced-group criterion gives smoothness; the diagonalizable geometric criteria also verify the split case.

source.place: Corollary 17.83 and its proof, p.379: choose a maximal torus over k; its existence under inclusion is expanded by dimension.

proof.text: In the nilpotent case, take the central torus $T$ and unipotent quotient $q:G\to Q$ with kernel $T$. Any torus $S$ containing $T$ has trivial map to $Q$: after splitting $S$ over $\bar k$, apply the diagonalizable-to-unipotent theorem, then descend the equality of coordinate maps by injectivity under field extension. Thus $S\subseteq\ker q=T$, so $T$ is maximal. Its centrality gives $C_G(T)=G$ on every algebra, and any $H$ in the assertion equals $G$. This includes unipotent groups, for which the maximal torus can be trivial.

source.place: Theorem 16.47, p.341, and first sentence of Theorem 17.91, p.381.

proof.text: Prove the generation assertion simultaneously for all smooth geometrically connected affine groups over $k$, by strong induction on their dimension $d$. For $d=0$ the trivial torus is maximal by step 2, and its centralizer is the whole group, proving the assertion. For $d>0$, assume the assertion for all groups of smaller dimension. First handle, at dimension $d$, groups for which the geometric Lie algebra has a noncentral semisimple element; call this the semisimple case. For such a group $V$, the tangent-span theorem supplies the nonempty family $K_X=C_V(X)^\circ$ of smooth geometrically connected proper subgroups of smaller dimension, whose tangent spaces span $\operatorname{Lie}(V)$.

source.place: Theorem 17.91, p.381: dimension induction and the infinite-field semisimple case. The base case and ordering of the same-dimension isogeny passage are made explicit.

proof.text: Let $H\subseteq V$ contain $C_V(T)$ for every maximal $k$-torus $T$ of $V$. For each $X$ in step 4 and each maximal torus $S\subseteq K_X$, the semisimple-centralizer maximal-torus theorem makes $S$ maximal in $V$. On every commutative algebra, an element of $C_{K_X}(S)$ also belongs to $C_V(S)$, hence to $H$. Thus $H\cap K_X$ is a closed subgroup of $K_X$ containing all its Cartan subgroups. The induction hypothesis applies to $K_X$ (strict dimension drop, same infinite base field) and gives $H\cap K_X=K_X$. Therefore $K_X\subseteq H$ for every $X$. No regularity is required of this intersection.

source.place: Proposition 17.90 and the last two sentences of the semisimple case of Theorem 17.91, p.381.

proof.text: Since $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(V)$ is finite-dimensional and the tangent spaces of step 4 span it, choose finitely many $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ among the indices of step 4 whose tangent spaces $\operatorname{Lie}(K_{X_j})\subseteq\mathfrak g$ already span $\mathfrak g$. Extend scalars to $\bar k$. Each $(K_{X_j})_{\bar k}$ and $V_{\bar k}$ is smooth by clause (2) of the base-change node and connected by geometric connectedness; they are affine of finite type, and $(K_{X_j})_{\bar k}\subseteq V_{\bar k}$ are closed subgroups. The dual-number calculus, applied with $R=\bar k$ and to the closed inclusions $K_{X_j}\subseteq V$, identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(J_{\bar k})=\ker(J(\bar k[\delta])\to J(\bar k))$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(J)\otimes_k\bar k$ naturally in $J$, so the images of $\operatorname{Lie}((K_{X_j})_{\bar k})$ span $\operatorname{Lie}(V_{\bar k})=\mathfrak g\otimes_k\bar k$. By step 5, $K_{X_j}\subseteq H$, hence $(K_{X_j})_{\bar k}\subseteq H_{\bar k}$, and $H_{\bar k}$ is a closed subgroup of $V_{\bar k}$ (a $\bar k$-algebra is a $k$-algebra). The tangent-generation theorem over the algebraically closed field $\bar k$, which allows a nonsmooth $H_{\bar k}$, gives $H_{\bar k}=V_{\bar k}$. If $I\subseteq k[V]$ is the ideal of $H$, then $I\otimes_k\bar k$ is the ideal of $H_{\bar k}$, hence zero, and injectivity of $I\to I\otimes_k\bar k$ (extend a basis) gives $I=0$. Thus $H=V$. This proves the semisimple case at dimension $d$, with arbitrary closed $H$.

source.place: Lie-spanning inference in Theorem 17.91, p.381, with Propositions 2.47 and 2.50, pp.55–56 (formation of the generated subgroup commutes with field extension).

proof.text: Now let $G$ be any group of dimension $d$. The infinitesimal-isogeny reduction gives a finite faithfully flat radicial homomorphism $f:G\to G\prime$ with $\dim G\prime=d$, where $G\prime$ is nilpotent or is in the semisimple case, and every $k$-torus of $G\prime$ lifts as the scheme-theoretic image of a $k$-torus of $G$. Its smooth connected target is geometrically connected by the rational identity criterion. Steps 3 and 6 have already proved the generation assertion for this particular $G\prime$ at dimension $d$; this is not an appeal to the induction hypothesis at the same dimension.

source.place: Proposition 17.80, p.378, inserted into Theorem 17.91, p.381, to handle the case omitted in the printed proof.

proof.text: Let $H\subseteq G$ contain all the Cartan subgroups. The affine homomorphism theorem gives its closed scheme-theoretic image $H\prime\subseteq G\prime$, with $H\to H\prime$ faithfully flat. Given a maximal $k$-torus $T\prime\subseteq G\prime$, lift it to a torus $T\subseteq G$ by step 7. The same homomorphism theorem makes $T\to T\prime$ faithfully flat, since $T\prime$ is its scheme-theoretic image. The radicial torus-centralizer comparison says both that $T$ is maximal in $G$ and that $C_G(T)\to C_{G\prime}(T\prime)$ is faithfully flat. Hence $C_{G\prime}(T\prime)\subseteq H\prime$: a function in the defining ideal of $H\prime$ pulls back to zero on $C_G(T)$, and faithful flatness makes its restriction to $C_{G\prime}(T\prime)$ zero. Thus $H\prime$ satisfies the generation hypothesis for $G\prime$. Step 7 gives $H\prime=G\prime$.

source.place: Agent-supplied isogeny passage from 17.80 to 17.91, using the scheme-theoretic homomorphism theorem 3.34, p.75, and torus-centralizer comparison.

proof.text: The map $H\to G\prime$ is now surjective, and it is finite: its coordinate algebra is a quotient of the finite $k[G\prime]$-module $k[G]$. The finite-surjective dimension theorem gives $\dim H=\dim G\prime=\dim G$. Apply step 1 to the closed subgroup $H\subseteq G$ to obtain $H=G$ as schemes. Together with maximal-torus existence in step 2, this proves every clause. This last argument uses neither smoothness nor connectedness of $H$, and never infers equality of arbitrary subgroup schemes from equality of their Lie algebras.

source.place: Completion of the omitted isogeny passage in Theorem 17.91, p.381; finite surjective dimension comparison and the dimension test in step 1.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 17.91, p.381, with Proposition 17.80, p.378, supplying the omitted bad-Lie-algebra case. Scheme-theoretic subgroup and isogeny assembly supplied explicitly.
